headings.title: Introduction and Epidemiology of STIs and HIV in Nigerian Adolescents
headings.content: Adolescent sexual and reproductive health remains a critical public health concern across Nigeria, with Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) and HIV/AIDS disproportionately affecting young people. Epidemiological data from the Federal Ministry of Health and international bodies indicate that adolescents and young adults account for a significant percentage of new HIV infections annually. This vulnerability is compounded by the country's youthful demographic structure, where individuals aged 10-24 make up a substantial portion of the population. Factors such as early sexual debut, multiple sexual partners, transactional sex driven by economic challenges, and inadequate access to comprehensive sexual education drive these high incidence rates. Furthermore, regional disparities exist across Nigeria, influenced by cultural norms, religious beliefs, and varying access to healthcare infrastructure. For nursing students, understanding the true epidemiological burden is essential for recognizing that adolescents are not merely a sub-group of the adult population, but a distinct demographic requiring targeted interventions. Healthcare facilities often report late presentations among youths due to fear of judgment and confidentiality breaches, leading to severe long-term complications including pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, and advanced HIV disease. Public health nursing strategies must therefore focus on community-based outreach, school health programs, and peer-led education to capture at-risk adolescents early. By analyzing these epidemiological trends, nursing professionals can better advocate for policy changes, resource allocation, and specialized adolescent health clinics tailored to the Nigerian context.

headings.title: Vulnerability Factors: Biological, Psychological, and Social Determinants
headings.content: The heightened vulnerability of Nigerian adolescents to STIs and HIV/AIDS is multi-faceted, stemming from an intricate intersection of biological, psychological, and social determinants. Biologically, adolescent females possess an immature cervical ectopy, meaning a larger area of the columnar epithelium is exposed to pathogens, significantly increasing their susceptibility to acquiring HIV and other STIs compared to mature adult women. Additionally, lower mucosal immune maturity and lower levels of protective vaginal flora place young girls at a higher biological risk. Psychologically, adolescence is characterized by identity formation, peer pressure, impulsivity, and the cognitive belief of invulnerability, which often translates into risk-taking behaviors such as unprotected sexual intercourse. Socially, poverty, gender inequality, harmful traditional practices, and poor parental communication about sex create an environment where young people cannot negotiate safe sex. In many Nigerian communities, girls may engage in transactional sex out of economic desperation to afford basic needs like school fees or sanitary pads. Societal stigma surrounding premarital sex and sexuality education further silences adolescents, preventing them from seeking timely information or preventive commodities like condoms. Nurses must evaluate all these domains during patient interactions, as addressing only the medical symptom without considering the underlying social or psychological driver will lead to repeated infections and poor health outcomes.

headings.title: Common Sexually Transmitted Infections in Youth: Presentation and Pathophysiology
headings.content: Common Sexually Transmitted Infections among youth in Nigeria include Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Trichomoniasis, Human Papillomavirus (HPV), Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV-2), and Syphilis. Many of these infections manifest with subtle symptoms or are entirely asymptomatic, particularly in females, which facilitates their silent transmission within peer networks. Pathophysiologically, bacterial infections like gonorrhea and chlamydia target the mucosal epithelium of the urethra, endocervix, and rectum, causing local inflammation, purulent discharge, and cellular damage. If left untreated, ascending infections lead to pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), chronic pelvic pain, ectopic pregnancy, and tubal factor infertility, which devastate future reproductive aspirations. Viral STIs such as HSV-2 cause painful vesicular lesions that break down into ulcers, serving as open portals of entry for HIV transmission. HPV strains, particularly types 16 and 18, integrate into host cellular DNA, increasing the long-term risk of cervical dysplasia and malignancies. Nurses caring for adolescents must recognize the clinical presentations—such as dysuria, abnormal vaginal or urethral discharge, lower abdominal pain, and genital lesions—and maintain a high index of suspicion. Syndromic management protocols are frequently utilized in resource-limited Nigerian settings where laboratory diagnostics are delayed, making comprehensive nursing assessments vital for administering timely, syndromic-based antibiotic therapy and partner notification services.

headings.title: HIV/AIDS Transmission Dynamics and Clinical Stages in Adolescents
headings.content: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) transmission among adolescents primarily occurs through unprotected heterosexual contact, mother-to-child transmission (perinatal transmission that survived into adolescence), blood transfusions, and sharing unsterilized sharp objects. Once the virus enters the body, it targets cells expressing CD4 receptors, predominantly T-helper lymphocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells. The pathophysiology involves viral entry, reverse transcription of viral RNA into DNA, integration into the host genome, and subsequent destruction of the immune system over time. Clinically, HIV infection progresses through distinct stages defined by the World Health Organization (WHO): acute primary infection, clinical stage 1 (asymptomatic or persistent generalized lymphadenopathy), stage 2 (mild symptoms such as minor mucocutaneous manifestations and recurrent upper respiratory infections), stage 3 (advanced symptoms including unexplained chronic diarrhea, persistent fever, and severe bacterial infections like pulmonary tuberculosis), and stage 4 (severe disease or AIDS-defining illnesses such as Kaposi's sarcoma, cryptococcal meningitis, and severe wasting syndrome). In adolescents, disease progression can sometimes be rapid due to hormonal shifts and adherence challenges, or conversely, slow if acquired perinatally with partial immune adaptation. Nurses must monitor adolescents closely for opportunistic infections characteristic of each clinical stage, provide thorough education on viral load suppression, and assess immunological markers like CD4 cell counts to evaluate disease progression and immune competence.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment, Screening, and Diagnostic Testing
headings.content: Comprehensive nursing assessment for adolescents presenting with suspected STIs or HIV requires a sensitive, non-judgmental, and confidential approach to build trust. Nurses must conduct a thorough sexual history—including age at sexual debut, number of partners, consistency of condom use, history of previous STIs, and experiences of forced or coerced sexual activity. Physical examination should be performed with utmost regard for privacy and trauma-informed care, inspecting for rashes, ulcers, discharge, lymphadenopathy, and signs of systemic illness. Screening and diagnostic testing protocols in Nigeria typically involve rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for HIV following serial testing algorithms, alongside laboratory investigations such as Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) tests for syphilis, wet mount preparations, cervical smears, and nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) where available. Pre-test and post-test counseling are mandatory components of the nursing process, ensuring that the adolescent understands the implications of testing, knows how to cope with a positive or negative result, and receives appropriate referrals. Nurses must also screen for psychological distress, depression, and suicidal ideation, which are notably prevalent among youths receiving a new diagnosis of a chronic infection like HIV. Documenting findings accurately and ensuring strict confidentiality in line with national healthcare guidelines protects the adolescent's rights and encourages continuous engagement with care.

headings.title: Clinical Management, Antiretroviral Therapy (ART), and Pharmacological Care
headings.content: Clinical management of HIV-positive adolescents centers around the lifelong administration of Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) aimed at achieving and maintaining viral suppression, restoring immune function, and preventing transmission. Current national guidelines in Nigeria recommend a Test and Treat approach, where ART is initiated immediately upon confirming an HIV diagnosis, regardless of CD4 count or clinical stage. First-line regimens usually consist of a combination of nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) coupled with an integrase strand transfer inhibitor (like dolutegravir) or a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (such as efavirenz). Pharmacological care by nurses involves educating adolescents on adherence, managing minor side effects (e.g., nausea, vivid dreams, fatigue), and monitoring for toxicities such as renal impairment, bone density loss, or metabolic abnormalities. Adherence is particularly challenging in the adolescent population due to busy school schedules, fear of accidental disclosure, pill fatigue, and developmental lifestyle changes. Nurses play a frontline role in adherence counseling, utilizing pillboxes, alarm reminders, peer support clubs, and Directly Observed Therapy (DOT) adaptations where necessary. Furthermore, management includes prompt treatment of opportunistic infections, routine viral load monitoring, nutritional counseling, and vaccination against preventable infections like Hepatitis B and Streptococcus pneumoniae.

headings.title: Adolescent-Friendly Health Services and Psychosocial Support
headings.content: Providing effective care for adolescents with STIs and HIV requires Adolescent-Friendly Health Services (AFHS) that reduce systemic barriers and respect youth autonomy. AFHS principles demand services that are accessible, acceptable, equitable, appropriate, and effective, featuring convenient operating hours, affordable or free services, and privacy-ensuring architectural designs. Healthcare providers must communicate respectfully without moralizing, condemning, or breaching patient confidentiality, which is a common deterrent keeping young people away from government hospitals. Psychosocial support is equally critical; nurses must integrate mental health assessments, counseling, and support groups (such as teen clubs) into routine care clinics. These groups offer safe spaces where adolescents living with HIV or recovering from recurrent STIs can share lived experiences, combat feelings of isolation, and learn positive coping mechanisms from peers facing similar health journeys. Additionally, nurses should involve family or trusted adult caregivers only when beneficial and appropriate, while respecting the legal and ethical boundaries of adolescent confidentiality and emancipated minor guidelines. By creating an empathetic, youth-centered healthcare environment, nursing professionals foster long-term treatment adherence, improve mental well-being, and empower adolescents to take charge of their sexual health.

headings.title: Prevention Strategies, Health Education, and Stigma Reduction
headings.content: Prevention of STIs and HIV/AIDS among Nigerian adolescents relies on robust, multi-layered strategies combining comprehensive health education, biomedical interventions, and intense stigma reduction campaigns. Comprehensive health education must be factual, age-appropriate, and culturally sensitive, delivered across schools, religious centers, and digital platforms to demystify sex, anatomy, and disease transmission. Biomedical prevention tools include the promotion and distribution of male and female condoms, Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) and Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) for high-risk individuals, and vaccination against HPV and Hepatitis B. Nurses play a crucial role as educators and advocates, teaching youths correct barrier methods, dispelling myths regarding HIV transmission (such as transmission through casual contact or mosquito bites), and normalizing discussions around sexual wellness. Equally important is tackling internal and external stigma and discrimination, which remains a formidable barrier preventing adolescents from seeking testing, treatment, and psychosocial support. Community sensitization programs led by healthcare teams can reframe public perceptions, emphasizing that STIs and HIV are manageable medical conditions rather than moral failings. By championing stigma reduction and proactive health education, nurses empower adolescents to protect themselves, practice safer behaviors, and support peers affected by these conditions.
